uncited: Transformer-based Reconstruction refers to a family of feed-forward neural network methods that directly predict 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from 2D image inputs, bypassing the iterative optimization required by standard 3DGS [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

Unlike iterative approaches that refine a scene representation over time, these models infer the scene geometry and appearance in a single forward pass, enabling real-time reconstruction from sparse or single views.

The family is distinguished from sibling rasterization and rendering optimizations by its focus on the generative reconstruction pipeline rather than the rendering speed or mathematical stability of the Gaussian primitives themselves.
**Input Modality**: The input consists of 2D images (monocular or multi-view) and, for multi-view methods, corresponding camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics) [S1, unofficial].

**Direct Parameter Prediction**: The network outputs the full set of 3D Gaussian parameters directly: mean position ($\mu$), covariance matrix ($\Sigma$), color ($c$), and opacity ($\alpha$) [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

**Transformer Architecture**: The core processing unit is a transformer block (or sequence of blocks) that attends to relationships between image features and camera poses to infer 3D structure [S1, unofficial].
**Feed-Forward Nature**: The reconstruction is non-iterative; the output is generated in a single inference step without gradient descent or scene optimization loops [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

**Supervision**: Training is supervised using photometric losses (e.g., LPIPS, SSIM) and potentially depth consistency losses, comparing rendered outputs against ground-truth input images [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].
The concept of feed-forward reconstruction for 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a solution to the computational bottleneck of iterative optimization in standard 3DGS [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].
Traditional 3DGS requires thousands of optimization steps to converge, making it unsuitable for real-time applications from sparse inputs.

Transformer-based methods leverage the attention mechanism's ability to model long-range dependencies and spatial relationships, allowing them to infer 3D structure from 2D projections directly [S1, unofficial].
Flash3D pioneered the monocular approach by integrating depth estimation into the Gaussian prediction pipeline [S1][S2, unofficial].
GS-LRM extended this to sparse multi-view settings by explicitly incorporating camera parameters into the transformer's token sequence [S1, unofficial].
These methods represent a shift from optimization-based reconstruction to learning-based direct prediction.
